acct_setup_rev_09_body: Bally feels like someone who actually hoops talking to you, not a robot. Real-time coaching on my release and balance changed my whole summer — smoother, more repeatable, no overthinking.

release_angle_message:
The release angle metric measures the trajectory of your shot in degrees, calculated from the point you release the ball.
            
A typical ideal angle for basketball shots is around 45 degrees, though it can vary depending on your shooting style and distance from the basket.
            
Understanding your release angle helps you fine-tune your form. Shots with a higher angle generally have a softer landing, reducing the risk of hitting the rim too hard and bouncing out.
            
On the other hand, flatter angles can lead to more direct hits, which may increase the chance of misses.
            
Tracking angle data over time allows you to adjust your form for greater consistency, especially when shooting from different spots on the court.
            
Whether you're working on free throws, jump shots, or three-pointers, keeping your angle consistent is key to improving shooting success.
release_time_message:
The release time metric measures the duration of your shot motion, from the beginning of your shooting motion to the moment the ball leaves your hand, recorded in seconds.
            
A faster shot release can be the difference between getting a clean shot off and having it blocked by a defender.
            
Speed and efficiency are key, especially in game scenarios where defenders are closing in quickly.
            
Tracking how long it takes you to complete your shot can highlight areas where you can tighten up your mechanics to speed up your release.
            
Consistently analyzing shot time allows you to gauge improvements in reaction time and shooting under pressure.
            
Over time, working on reducing your shot duration will help you develop a quicker, more efficient shot without sacrificing accuracy.

The shot force metric measures the power behind your shot in newtons. This value is derived from the amount of force your wrist generates when propelling the ball toward the hoop.
            
Monitoring force is crucial for developing shooting precision. Too much force might cause the ball to hit the back of the rim or overshoot entirely, while too little force can cause shots to fall short.
            
By keeping track of how much power you're putting into your shots, you can start to identify patterns in your misses, such as shots that are consistently too hard or too soft.
            
Consistent shot force is especially important when shooting from long range or under pressure, where it’s easy to apply too much or too little power. Balancing strength with finesse will help you become a more reliable shooter.
